title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Tracheoinnominate fistula represents a rare but devastating complication most frequently associated with tracheostomy, carrying mortality rates that may exceed 50% even with intervention. The condition arises when erosion occurs between the trachea and the innominate artery, leading to massive hemorrhage that can be rapidly fatal. Although tracheostomy is the most common cause, tracheoinnominate fistula has also been reported following tracheal resection, penetrating neck trauma, endovascular stent placement, or migration of orthopedic hardware. A sentinel or herald bleed—typically a brief, self-limited hemorrhage—often precedes catastrophic bleeding, serving as a critical warning sign. Differentiating this presentation from more benign causes of hemoptysis or stomal bleeding requires heightened clinical suspicion. Successful outcomes depend on prompt recognition, rapid airway protection, and urgent surgical or endovascular repair. Delay in diagnosis or misattribution of early warning signs can quickly lead to uncontrolled exsanguination and death, making awareness of this complication essential for clinicians managing patients with tracheostomies or tracheal procedures.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: The course prepares clinicians to recognize and manage tracheoinnominate fistula, focusing on timely diagnosis, emergency stabilization, and definitive treatment. Participants learn to identify high-risk features, acknowledge the importance of sentinel bleeding, and apply appropriate diagnostic strategies that distinguish tracheoinnominate fistula from other posttracheostomy complications. Instruction emphasizes evidence-based approaches to surgical and endovascular repair and addresses the role of rapid airway management in the stabilization process. Collaboration with an interprofessional team—including surgeons, intensivists, respiratory therapists, and nursing staff—is a key determinant of improved outcomes. By strengthening clinical knowledge and enhancing interprofessional teamwork, the course equips participants to reduce mortality and deliver high-quality, patient-centered care to those affected by this life-threatening complication.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Introduction
content: Tracheoinnominate fistula is a rare but life-threatening complication most frequently associated with tracheostomy, carrying a high risk of massive hemorrhage and mortality. This condition has also been reported following tracheal resection and reconstruction, penetrating neck trauma, and migration of orthopedic hardware, and, rarely, after endovascular stent graft placement. [1] [2] [3] The innominate artery, also known as the brachiocephalic artery or trunk, is one of the three principal branches of the aortic arch. This artery courses cephalad and anterior to the trachea, deep to the sternum, ultimately bifurcating into the right common carotid and subclavian arteries. The proximity to the trachea makes it vulnerable to injury during tracheostomy and other endotracheal procedures. [4] A fistula may develop from direct intraoperative injury or as a delayed complication due to pressure necrosis from the tracheostomy tube or cuff, resulting in catastrophic hemorrhage. [5] [6]

[4] A fistula may develop from direct intraoperative injury or as a delayed complication due to pressure necrosis from the tracheostomy tube or cuff, resulting in catastrophic hemorrhage. [5] [6]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Etiology
content: Several factors can predispose patients to the development of a tracheoinnominate fistula. Gradual pressure necrosis of the tracheal and arterial walls is recognized as the most common mechanism, with aberrant communication and massive hemorrhage resulting thereafter. Tracheoinnominate fistula most often arises in the setting of a tracheostomy, where cuff pressures exceeding 20 to 30 cm H 2 O may reduce mucosal perfusion and promote necrosis. [7] Additional risk factors include malposition of the rigid tracheostomy tube, impingement of the solid tracheostomy tube against the manubrium, and repeated mucosal trauma from tube movement, such as in patients with seizure disorders. [8] [9]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Etiology
content: Anatomical factors may also predispose patients to developing a tracheoinnominate fistula, with a high-riding innominate artery being the most recognized. This standard anatomical variant occurs when the brachiocephalic trunk (innominate artery) bifurcates more cephalad than usual, sometimes above the sternoclavicular joint. [10] In this position, the vessel lies near the proximal trachea, increasing vulnerability during tracheostomy or prolonged intubation. [11]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Etiology
content: Protection of the innominate is crucial regardless of its anatomic position, which provides the rationale for placing the tracheostomy incision as proximally as feasible. Tracheostomy placement distal to the third tracheal ring (low tracheostomy) carries an increased risk of tracheoinnominate fistula, even when the innominate artery occupies its typical anatomic location. [12] More rarely, tracheoinnominate fistula may arise from unrecognized vascular or tracheal injury during open neck or mediastinum surgical procedures, or from migration of endovascular stents or orthopaedic hardware. [1] [13] [14] Other common causes include penetrating neck trauma, infection, prior radiation therapy, and direct tumor erosion. [15] [16] [17]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Epidemiology
content: The incidence of tracheoinnominate fistula ranges from 0.1% to 1% of tracheostomies. [18] [19] Most cases (about 70%) occur within the first 3 weeks, with a peak incidence between 7 and 14 days after the procedure. However, delayed presentations have been documented, including cases developed more than 1 year after tracheostomy. [18]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Pathophysiology
content: The innominate artery typically traverses the trachea between the sixth and ninth tracheal rings. Accordingly, tracheostomy placement below the third tracheal ring increases the risk of tracheoinnominate fistula. Overinflation of the tracheostomy cuff is another recognized risk, with pressures exceeding 30 cm H 2 O historically linked to impaired mucosal blood flow, leading to continued pressure necrosis and erosion into the posterior segment of the innominate artery. [20] Additional risk factors include prior neck irradiation and recurrent hypotension, which compromise mucosal microcirculation and promote necrosis. [1] Systemic corticosteroid use has also been associated with increased risk of tracheoinnominate fistula, presumably due to impaired wound healing and local tissue repair. [21]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- History and Physical
content: Patients with tracheoinnominate fistula nearly always have a prior history of tracheostomy, with risk following both percutaneous and open procedures. [22] Up to 35% of patients develop a sentinel or herald bleed, a small volume of bleeding occurring 24 to 48 hours before massive hemorrhage. [21] Clinical presentation often includes sudden, large-volume pulsatile bleeding from the tracheostomy site, hemoptysis with potential airway compromise, or febrile episodes. Patients may rapidly deteriorate, developing hemodynamic instability and hemorrhagic shock owing to the severity of bleeding. [23] Most cases occur within 1 to 6 weeks of tracheostomy placement, with 50 % to 75% presenting between 1 and 2 weeks postoperatively. [24]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination should begin with assessing vital signs to evaluate hemodynamic stability, followed by a general mental and respiratory status evaluation. Careful inspection of the neck and tracheostomy site is essential, with attention to the amount and character of bleeding. In the setting of active, high-volume, or pulsatile bleeding, immediate consultation with thoracic surgery is arranged while resuscitative efforts are initiated. If bleeding is absent or low in volume, otolaryngocoly consultation should be obtained for endoscopic evaluation of the trachea and formal assessment of the tracheostomy site.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Evaluation
content: Urgent evaluation and treatment are crucial to improving outcomes in tracheoinnominate fistula. Diagnostic modalities include bronchoscopy, conventional angiography, and computed tomography angiography, though each has limited sensitivity for diagnosing the condition. Therefore, maintaining a high index of clinical suspicion, supported by thorough history and physical examination, is critical.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Evaluation
content: Low-volume or venous-appearing bleeding, particularly from a recent tracheostomy, is more commonly due to surgery-related venous oozing, and often from the thyroid or skin edges, rather than a true tracheoinnominate fistula. [25] On bronchoscopy, direct visualization of the active bleeding site on the anterior wall of the trachea may be observed. Angiography and computed tomography angiography may reveal contrast extravasation or a vascular blush from the innominate artery into the trachea, though reported sensitivity is only 20% to 30%. [26] [27] [28]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: Immediate management is critical and depends on the prompt recognition of tracheoinnominate fistula. Hemorrhage can be temporarily controlled using the Utley maneuver, in which a finger is inserted through the tracheostomy incision to compress the innominate artery against the posterior sternum. A similar tamponade effect can be achieved by overinflating the tracheostomy cuff. [29] Additional assistance should be summoned immediately, as simultaneous control of the airway and bleeding requires multiple providers. The placement of a cuffed endotracheal tube distal to the bleeding site is the most effective temporary measure. Blood products should be made rapidly available in anticipation of massive transfusion.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: Currently, most institutions have a massive transfusion protocol that can be quickly activated. Depending on the institution, management of tracheoinnominate fistula may be spearheaded by trauma and acute care surgery, cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery, or vascular surgery teams. Definitive management can be achieved either through open surgical techniques or endovascular approaches. [30]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: The open surgical approach typically involves median sternotomy, or a variation such as a collar incision with a partial sternotomy, followed by ligation and division of the innominate artery. [31] Ligation without division of the innominate artery is contraindicated because the artery can re-fistulize. [32] Sometimes, the innominate artery may need to be buttressed with a patch of pericardium or vein, though cotton pledgets can also be used. The tracheal defect is typically covered with a local or regional flap, most commonly the pectoralis major muscle. [33] Extensive tracheal resection or reconstruction is rarely necessary. Additional protective materials against infection may include pericardium, thymus, or pleura. Neurologic complications occur in up to 10% of patients following ligation of the innominate artery. [32] Despite the risk, survival depends on rapid hemorrhage control, and the procedure remains the standard lifesaving intervention in most cases.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: Some authors have described revascularization procedures such as innominate-to-carotid, aorta-to-innominate, aorta-to-axillary, or carotid-to-carotid artery bypass. However, these approaches are not considered standard practice due to the heightened risk of infection in the setting of tracheoinnominate fistula. When performed, various graft materials have been successfully employed, including synthetic grafts (eg, polytetrafluoroethylene), cryopreserved arterial allografts, and autologous vein grafts. Postoperative complications include mediastinitis, fistulization, and sternal wound infection. [5] [27] [34]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: Endovascular techniques have also been successfully employed, particularly in patients who are prohibitively high-risk for open surgery.These approaches may be preferable in patients with a history of a median sternotomy, thoracotomy, or prior neck or chest irradiation. [35] Successful endovascular stent-graft placement requires selective catheterization of the innominate artery and adequate seal zones. [36]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: Some authors have described hybrid procedures employing endovascular and open surgical techniques. In these cases, such as a carotid-subclavian bypass, a surgical bypass is performed along with the placement of an endograft stent, as the bypass provides longer landing zones. [37] The stent can be placed via the femoral artery or through direct cutdown on other vessels such as the carotid, brachial, or axillary arteries. Completion angiography is performed after the procedure to confirm technical success. Complications of hybrid procedures include access site complications, such as hematoma; stent migration; maldeployment; or fracture. Recurrent tracheoinnominate fistula has been reported in the setting of a stent-graft fracture. [38] Additionally, inadequate seal zones may result in endoleak, leading to persistent hemorrhage.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Treatment / Management
content: In select cases, endovascular stenting may be used as a bridge to stabilize the critically ill patient, allowing time for resuscitation and eventual definitive open surgical intervention in an elective or semi-elective setting. In critically ill individuals with ongoing bleeding, temporary control can also be achieved by placing an occlusion balloon (eg, Fogarty catheter) in the innominate artery under fluoroscopic guidance, via either transfemoral or transbrachial routes. [39] This maneuver can be lifesaving, providing time to mobilize resources for definitive intervention. Additionally, some authors have described coil embolization of the innominate artery under fluoroscopy combined with selective bypass procedures to preserve cerebral circulation.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Bleeding around the tracheostomy site may be mistaken for hemorrhage from stomal granulation tissue. Early postoperative bleeding is more commonly related to inadequate procedural hemostasis or underlying coagulopathy.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Prognosis
content: Patients should be monitored closely in the intensive care unit after intervention, as rebleeding may occur despite apparently successful procedures. Prognosis remains guarded even with prompt recognition and treatment. Most patients are critically ill and debilitated at the time of the hemorrhagic event, often with multiple comorbidities; perioperative mortality exceeds 50%. [19]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Complications
content: Because tracheoinnominate fistula is itself a complication, most often of tracheostomy surgery, a few additional complications are described. However, if left untreated, tracheoinnominate fistula is uniformly fatal, with a mortality rate of 100%. [40]

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Tracheoinnominate fistula should be prevented through meticulous technique and careful postoperative management. Recommended measures include: Limiting the duration of endotracheal intubation to less than 3 weeks. Using proper technique during tracheostomy placement. Selecting blunt, flexible tracheostomy tubes. Positioning the tracheostomy between the second and third tracheal rings. Minimizing repetitive head and neck movements to reduce contact between the underside of the tube and the innominate artery.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Tracheoinnominate fistula is a rare but often fatal complication if unrecognized. Awareness of this condition is essential for clinicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists caring for patients with a tracheostomy. Prevention remains the key. A flexible, appropriately long connecter tube should be attached to the tracheostomy to allow mobility and minimize stress on the site.

title: Tracheoinnominate Fistula  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Any observation of bright red bleeding around the tracheostomy or palpable pulsations of the tracheostomy tube should prompt immediate notification of the surgical team. Tracheal cuff pressures must be monitored regularly, and all bleeding from the tracheostomy site must be reported to the critical care physician. If tracheoinnominate fistula is suspected, the nurse, respiratory therapist, and clinician must promptly secure the airway and control bleeding until thoracic surgical consultation is obtained. Any observation of bright red bleeding around the tracheostomy or palpable pulsations of the tracheostomy tube should prompt immediate notification of the surgical team. Tracheal cuff pressures must be monitored regularly, and all bleeding from the tracheostomy site must be reported to the critical care physician. If tracheoinnominate fistula is suspected, the nurse, respiratory therapist, and clinician must promptly secure the airway and control bleeding until thoracic surgical consultation is obtained.
